title: Every soccer-mom needs to see this ☝️
body: WARNING: I made a huge mistake after buying Footstr insoles for my son. Don't do what I did. I almost threw them away. Three weeks after they arrived, I nearly pulled them out of his cleats and tossed them in the trash. Not because they weren't working. Because of what happened after he started wearing them. Let me explain. My son is 9, he plays soccer, and somewhere over the past year I had quietly accepted that sore feet were just part of who he was. The slow limp to the car after practice. The ankles rolling inward every time he stood barefoot. Me planning our weekends around how much his feet could handle. Our doctor looked at his flat feet, shrugged, and said he'd probably grow out of it. So I went down the internet rabbit hole. That's when I found Footstr. Insoles made for kids who overpronate, with flexible arch support, heel cushioning, and a foot strengthening program. Honestly, it seemed too simple. We had already spent $450 on custom orthotics. What was a kids' insole going to do that those couldn't? But the reviews from other soccer parents sounded exactly like my house. So I ordered. ===== MY FIRST MISTAKE I didn't tell my husband. Not because he wouldn't be supportive. I just didn't want to get his hopes up. Or mine. I pulled the old orthotic out of my son's cleat, slid the Footstr in, and handed him the shoe like it was nothing. By week two, something strange happened. He was still wearing them. That might sound small, but the $450 custom orthotics lasted about two weeks before I started finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag. He hated how hard they felt under his feet. The Footstrs just stayed in his shoes. School, practice, the park. I never had to argue once. And I noticed something else. He stopped kicking his shoes off the second he got in the car. ===== THE REAL PROBLEM STARTED IN WEEK THREE Saturday game. Normally I watch the second half differently than the other parents. I'm not watching the ball. I'm watching my son's run, waiting for it to turn into that heavy, flat-footed jog that means his feet are done. But this time? Nothing happened. He just... played. The whole game. Afterward he walked to the car talking about a goal he almost scored, and climbed in like a kid whose feet had never once been a topic in our family. That night after dinner, he asked my husband to go kick the ball around in the yard. I tensed up. Evenings were usually when his feet and legs were finished for the day. But before I could say "maybe tomorrow," he was already outside. ===== HERE'S WHERE I ALMOST MADE MY BIGGEST MISTAKE That next week, I caught myself watching him constantly. Waiting for the limp to come back. Waiting for him to wake up with sore legs again. Waiting for the other shoe to drop. And when it didn't, I did something ridiculous. I decided it couldn't be the insoles. I nearly took them out and put the custom orthotics back in. The expensive ones. The prescribed ones. The "real" ones. Because somewhere along the way, I'd been trained to believe that if a solution isn't expensive and complicated, it can't actually be doing anything. $450 and a specialist appointment felt serious. A comfortable insole my kid actually liked wearing felt too easy. I'm so glad I stopped myself. Because the customs never really had a chance to help him. They were so stiff and bulky inside his cleats that he wouldn't keep them on his feet. And support sitting at the bottom of a soccer bag isn't supporting anything. ===== WHAT I FINALLY LEARNED That was the week I sat down and actually researched what was going on with his feet. I found a study of 92,000 adolescents. The ones with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches. Another study from 2025 looked at school aged kids specifically. Children with flat feet scored 42 percent higher on a clinical pain scale than their classmates, and they were measurably less active because of it. Neither study proved that my son's feet were behind every complaint he ever had. But they explained something I'd been watching for a year without understanding it. When his arch rolled inward under his weight, his whole leg was working from a wobbly base. Every sprint, every cut, every landing started from a foot that collapsed a little with each step. Then I finally read what was actually behind the Footstr design. Structured arch support that flexes as he runs instead of locking his foot in place the way the customs did. It helps reduce that excessive inward rolling while he's wearing them. Heel cushioning, so all the pounding from running and jumping has a softer place to land. And the part I didn't appreciate when I ordered: the strengthening program. The insole and the exercises have two different jobs. The insole supports his arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet and arches something to work on outside the shoe as he grows. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. This wasn't just a softer version of the orthotics. It was the first thing that felt like a plan instead of another thing we bought after he was already hurting. ===== THE SIDE EFFECT NOBODY WARNS YOU ABOUT About two months in, my husband said something on the drive home from a game that stuck with me. "He hasn't stopped talking since he got in the car." He was right. I hadn't realized how quiet those drives had gotten over the past year. How much of our family's energy went into managing his feet. The ice, the rest days, the bargaining over whether he could handle practice. I'm not going to tell you his feet became indestructible. He still gets tired. He still has sore days after a big tournament. But the sore days stopped running our week. ===== WHY MOST "SOLUTIONS" NEVER WORKED FOR US Before Footstr, we tried the whole list. Custom orthotics. To be fair, when he actually wore them, his ankles didn't roll inward as badly. But they were rigid, bulky inside his cleats, $450, and he'd outgrow them within the year. Support your kid refuses to wear isn't support. Pharmacy inserts. Soft, cheap, and completely flat. They just followed his foot down as the arch collapsed. Rest. His feet always felt better after a week off. And the complaints always came back once he was playing again. Better shoes. They helped a little. But the support stayed home every time he switched into his cleats. None of it dealt with what was happening underneath him. A foot rolling inward under his weight, step after step, all day long. ===== WHAT I WISH SOMEONE HAD TOLD ME SOONER If your kid's ankles roll inward when they stand. If their shoes wear down faster along the inside edge. If they limp after practice, ask to sit out, or say their feet are tired before they are. Please don't spend a year like I did, telling yourself it's just growing pains. And if you do try something and things start getting better, don't make my mistake. Don't talk yourself out of it just because it was simple. Right now Footstr is running their Back to School sale, and everything is 60% off. We paid $450 for orthotics that lived in a soccer bag. These cost a fraction of that, and they're actually on my son's feet every day. Click below to see Footstr 👇 https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex One last thing, from one parent to another. I spent three weeks waiting for the bad news to come back before I let myself believe the good news. Watching your kid walk to the car talking about the game instead of his feet... you're allowed to believe that. I only wish we'd found them sooner.
